{"id": "7:20/q24", "question": "Does the promised angelhood prove angels superior to humans or prophets?", "turns_on": "Whether desiring an angelic quality entails conceding an overall hierarchy.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q24/p1", "position": "It suggests angels occupy a higher rank.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Naḥḥās infer superiority; al-Naḥḥās invokes 11:31 and 4:172, al-Ḥasan points to form, wings, and honor, and another account cites obedience and freedom from sin. Islāḥī says Adam regarded angels as higher."}, {"id": "7:20/q24/p2", "position": "It does not establish absolute superiority over humans or prophets.", "reasons": "Ibn Fūrak says angelhood might mean no appetite for food; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī mention innate traits. Al-Rāzī says Adam may not yet have been a prophet, or may have sought power, light, or proximity, not rank; he notes angels had prostrated to Adam. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Zajjāj and others favor believers; al-Kalbī excepts four named angels."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q25", "question": "Who are al-khālidīn?", "turns_on": "Whether khulūd promises endless earthly life, a long stay, or life after resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q25/p1", "position": "Those who never die and remain forever in the Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Wahb, and later commentators give this gloss; Ibn ʿAbbās says if they missed angelhood they would still never die there. Asad translates 'those who endure.'"}, {"id": "7:20/q25/p2", "position": "Khulūd can mean prolonged life rather than endless duration.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī uses this to answer the claim that Adam's acceptance would deny resurrection; al-Ālūsī echoes it."}, {"id": "7:20/q25/p3", "position": "It may mean enduring life after death in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this resolution but says it departs from the apparent sense."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q26", "question": "What is conveyed by min al-khālidīn instead of just khālidīn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q26/p1", "position": "Membership in the enduring group strengthens the promise.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn compares 66:12."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q27", "question": "Does aw offer a choice or both promised benefits?", "turns_on": "The scope of aw: alternative outcomes or a cumulative inducement.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q27/p1", "position": "It presents two possible alternatives without implying doubt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says both may be possible or one excluded; al-Rāzī reports a literal choice. Muqātil says if not angels, then immortal."}, {"id": "7:20/q27/p2", "position": "It offers angelhood and immortality together.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports that combined benefits heighten temptation."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q28", "question": "Did the pair believe Satan's claim?", "turns_on": "Whether eating implies assent and what Adam could yet know about death.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q28/p1", "position": "They ate under desire without believing or even probably assenting to him.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says belief would have been unbelief; al-Rāzī prefers desire as sufficient motive and reports careful scholars denying assent. Al-Samarrāʾī reports Adam saying he had not expected a false oath by God."}, {"id": "7:20/q28/p2", "position": "Their taking immortality literally need not imply disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says khulūd may be long life; even eternal life need not deny known revelation if mortality had not yet been disclosed. Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise says death and resurrection are learned by revelation; al-Ālūsī repeats the answer."}, {"id": "7:20/q28/p3", "position": "They may have been persuaded by repeated deceptive approaches.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says knowing Iblis as enemy did not make Adam immune to persistence; Muqātil reports Iblis claiming prior creation and superior knowledge. Al-Bursawī says he first mourned their coming death and separation."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q29", "question": "Why did the promised benefits tempt them?", "turns_on": "Whether their longing is read as personal gain, the wish for divine company, or a warning against greed.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q29/p1", "position": "Angelic qualities and lasting life appeared desirable.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī names elevated status and eternal delight; al-Qushayrī names freedom from desire; Elmalılı describes envy and a material route to life. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Satan offered one or both benefits; Study Quran calls false hope a satanic tactic. Al-Māwardī says they knew God fully but not all His rulings, allowing temptation; Asad says the wish to live forever promised likeness to God (20:120)."}, {"id": "7:20/q29/p2", "position": "They sought lasting life with God, not private gain.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī prefers this to an interpretation of greed because of prophetic dignity."}, {"id": "7:20/q29/p3", "position": "Their desire for permanence exposed the danger of greed.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says it produced abasement, ordeal, and fear; the danger is greater in transient life."}, {"id": "7:20/q29/p4", "position": "Only permanence, rather than angelic rank, drew them.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites the parallel in Ṭā Hā, where lasting life is promised before the eating."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q30", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from the whisper and exposure?", "turns_on": "Different inward applications of the same narrative.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q30/p1", "position": "Whispering moves from natural inclination through the self into inward thought and planning.", "reasons": "Sahl is transmitted by al-Tustarī and al-Sulamī; al-Tustarī also describes enemy prompting as invitation, confidence after acceptance, then waiting for an opening."}, {"id": "7:20/q30/p2", "position": "An evil whisper can become the occasion of repentance and divine favor.", "reasons": "Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī says Satan meant evil, while Adam's lapse disciplined him and led to confession in 7:23; al-Qushayrī sees divine care in attributing the lapse to Satan."}, {"id": "7:20/q30/p3", "position": "Worldly sensory benefit masquerades as angelic pleasure and lasting rule.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads bodily nature as counterfeit angelic perception and its king reading as rule over faculties and animals; 20:120 echoes the promise."}, {"id": "7:20/q30/p4", "position": "Loss of union after hoped-for permanence makes the episode a lesson in separation.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports entry in morning and exit at midday, a poetic evil-eye comparison, and another poem on hidden separation destroying gathered joy."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q31", "question": "How does this account connect to the surrounding clothing passages and other retellings?", "turns_on": "How 7:20 functions amid the exposure, clothing, and parallel Garden narratives.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q31/p1", "position": "The exposure leads into the leaf-covering and clothing warning.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī invokes 7:27 and al-Samarrāʾī links 7:22 to 7:26: clothing veils outer nakedness and piety inner faults. Study Quran compares 20:118–121 and 7:22, 26–32, and the Biblical sequence; the warning addresses Adam's descendants."}, {"id": "7:20/q31/p2", "position": "Al-Aʿrāf's fuller whisper scene makes Satan's scheme vivid for its audience.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān contrasts al-Baqara's 'caused them to slip' with al-Aʿrāf's whisper. Ibn ʿĀshūr says al-Aʿrāf addressed polytheists needing this detail; al-Jishumī attributes repeated stories to changing audiences over twenty-odd years and to varied inimitable expression."}, {"id": "7:20/q31/p3", "position": "The broader Garden account is treated as a test of human nature.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī places Adam in a heavenly intermediate garden before earthly law, neither eternal Paradise nor ordinary earthly life; humanity matures under commands after descent. He points readers to al-Baqara and interprets Adam as humanity's representative."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q32", "question": "What does the episode teach about Satan's agency and human responsibility?", "turns_on": "What larger lesson sources attach to the temptation.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q32/p1", "position": "Satan seeks disobedience through persuasive falsehood while the pair remain responsible.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says envy drove deception; al-Islāḥī connects the granted respite to access. Al-Qushayrī reports Adam's rebuke and Satan's reply asking about Adam's own devil. Study Quran says Satan whispers and commands indecency."}, {"id": "7:20/q32/p2", "position": "The story also figures the order of creation and the original sin of pride.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣādiq calls Iblis's first sin egotism or arrogance; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reconciles the reports. ʿAlī's sermon says Iblis and hosts resisted the prostration command through pride; Jaʿfar and al-Ṣādiq warn against religious analogy after Iblis's fire/clay analogy. ʿAlī calls him the first disbeliever."}, {"id": "7:20/q32/p3", "position": "Satan is an unseen influence requiring thoughtful attention.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī criticizes casual cursing or attribution of thoughts without reflecting on the Qurʾānic account; al-Ṣādiq compares devils' pressure on believers to wasps on meat; al-Riḍā derives Iblis from despair."}]}
{"id": "7:20/q33", "question": "What wider reports illustrate satanic prompting and seeking protection?", "turns_on": "The reported examples and lexical parallels cited around satanic whispering.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q33/p1", "position": "The reports describe jinn, devils, and refuge prayers in varied settings.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites warnings about household jinn, the Night Journey afrit and Gabriel's prayer, Kaʿb's refuge formula, Khālid's nightmare prayer, the Prophet's recitation to jinn, Jesus' vision of Satan at the heart, Satan flowing like blood, and a report that everyone has a satan. He explains aʿūdhu as seeking protection or clinging to grace, rajīm as cursed or pelted, and the Hearing/Knowing formula by God's knowledge of hidden whispers or Qurʾāni

{"id": "7:20/q34", "question": "What broader language and rhetoric principles are invoked in discussing Qurʾānic wording?", "turns_on": "Different general principles and reports supplied alongside this verse's language.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q34/p1", "position": "Explicit naming and repetition can convey force that pronouns or allusion do not.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir cites Abū Yaʿqūb, Dhū al-Rumma's line, and 17:105, 112:1–2; al-Jāḥiẓ's account of Qays ibn Khārija supplies a speech example."}, {"id": "7:20/q34/p2", "position": "Poetry witnesses rare Arabic usage, with debate over how many synonyms Arabic has.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says Ibn ʿAbbās used poetry as the Arabs' register and demanded more witnesses for doctrinal words; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports synonym and distinction schools, al-Aṣmaʿī's stone terms, Ibn Khālawayh's animal and sword terms, and Abū ʿAlī's objection that many are adjectives."}, {"id": "7:20/q34/p3", "position": "Qurʾānic eloquence and interpretation depend on discernment and transmitted explanation.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī discusses grief in preceding speech, creative commands (36:82, 7:166, 26:63), al-Buḥturī and Musaylima, the Prophet's comparison of divine speech, and literary training. Al-Burhān says Qurʾān and hadith mutually clarify; Ibn Barjān finds a Qurʾānic basis even for the stoning judgment."}, {"id": "7:20/q34/p4", "position": "The refuge surahs' Qurʾānic status rests on sound transmission despite a reported codex omission.", "reasons": "Al-Nawawī states consensus, Ibn Ḥazm calls the contrary story fabricated, al-Bāqillānī limits the objection to codex inscription, and Zirr reports Ubayy's account of Gabriel teaching the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q01", "question": "What does al-qist mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether qist is read as broad equity and balance, its foremost instance of monotheism, an exhaustive label for obedience, or an inward virtue; the root's derivation is also disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q01/p1", "position": "Justice, fairness, truth, or the balanced and upright course in all affairs.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Zajjaj, Ibn Abi Hatim, Thalabi, Qushayri, Wahidi, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabarsi, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Bursawi, Alusi, Elmalili, Ibn Ashur, Islahi, Kuranyolu and Study Quran give justice/fairness. Zajjaj, Razi, Nasafi call it rationally recognizable good; Baydawi, Bursawi, Alusi, Elmalili and Ibn Ashur explain a mean between excess and deficiency, with Bursawi citing a report and Persian verse. Mawrdi and Abu Hayyan add truth/right. Jishumi relates it to direction toward truth, with 5:42 and 72:15; Tabarsi similarly contrasts inclination to truth with falsehood (60:8, 72:15). Alusi prefers Raghib's allotment derivation: qasata takes another's share unjustly, aqsata gives it fairly, against Tabarsi's inclination etymology; Tabatabai also transmits Raghib. Ibn Ashur gives monotheism, retaliation, beneficence, clothing and food as balanced examples (25:67). Islahi extends balance to belief, morals, worship, economics, politics and society. Kuranyolu includes truth in belief and conduct."}, {"id": "7:29/q01/p2", "position": "The testimony that there is no god but God, or monotheism.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas supplies the shahada, Dahhak monotheism, and Razi cites 3:18; Abu Hayyan says all good begins with it. Ibn Ashur regards monotheism as a supreme instance of justice rather than its whole scope; Kuranyolu cites 31:13 against shirk. Razi makes the first command encompass knowledge of God's essence, acts, rulings and oneness; Study Quran links 3:18."}, {"id": "7:29/q01/p3", "position": "A comprehensive name for every praiseworthy act of obedience and devotion.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim calls it all good/obedience; Tabarsi says this is the positive command after indecency is denied; Biqai specifies obligations, established by reason and transmission. Islahi says it underlies every religious directive."}, {"id": "7:29/q01/p4", "position": "Truthfulness.", "reasons": "Abu Uthman supplies this inward gloss."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q02", "question": "How does the command to justice answer the previous claim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q02/p1", "position": "God commands justice and good, refuting the claim that He commanded indecency, especially naked circumambulation and inherited pagan customs.", "reasons": "Zajjaj appeals to rational recognition that ugly acts cannot be just. Wahidi cites 7:28; Jishumi says the passage then moves to promise and threat. Razi says justice is good by qualities intrinsic to it, though he refers to his earlier answer on intrinsic good. Ibn Ashur says repeated 'say' emphasizes the denial, and commanding the contrary also implicitly forbids indecency. Tabatabai calls the command the opposite of the prior claim. Durr's Qatada says God neither commands nor approves disobedience. Kuranyolu rejects sanctifying inherited wrongs; Ibn Ashur specifically considers clothing and food."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q03", "question": "What does justice require in practice?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q03/p1", "position": "It requires fairness toward God, others, and oneself, moderation in conduct, and worship of God alone.", "reasons": "Qushayri specifies duties, prohibitions and preferring nothing to God; fair dealing with people, sometimes relinquishing one's claim; and disciplining the soul. Ibn Ashur treats monotheism, measured retaliation, beneficence, clothing and food as examples. Islahi extends fairness through religious and public life and says the Creator's rights entail exclusive worship and accountability; absent recompense would be unjust. Kuranyolu rejects deifying ancestors and serving misguided leaders. Tabatabai rejects idolatry and blind imitation."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q04", "question": "How is the imperative 'establish' joined syntactically to 'my Lord commanded'?", "turns_on": "Which unspoken command or reporting verb licenses an imperative after the statement 'my Lord commanded justice'.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q04/p1", "position": "It coordinates with the implied imperative 'be just' or with an expanded verbal noun meaning 'that you be just.'", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Samīn and Tabatabai derive 'be just' from the command to justice. Samīn prefers this, explaining that an can unpack a verbal noun with past, present or imperative (the verse about wearing a cloak and pleasing the eye illustrates present), whereas ma cannot join an imperative and kay takes only present. Abu Hayyan supplies an plus the imperative and rejects a merely nominal masdar particle. Qurtubi notes the ellipsis."}, {"id": "7:29/q04/p2", "position": "An omitted 'say' introduces the imperative, either repeated independently or coordinated with the first 'say.'", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi, Razi, Abu Hayyan/Samīn on Zamakhshari, and Bursawi supply 'and say'; Bursawi avoids directly coordinating imperative and indicative. Wahidi's Jurjani says the Lord's command is speech, so the sense is 'say: God says, be just and establish.' Samīn also records attaching the imperative to the reported 'my Lord commanded' within the governing 'say.'"}, {"id": "7:29/q04/p3", "position": "An omitted 'and [He commanded] that you establish' links it to the previous command.", "reasons": "Jishumi supplies the conjunction and verbal noun. Alusi records this among several possible attachments."}, {"id": "7:29/q04/p4", "position": "It coordinates with another implied imperative, such as 'turn toward God' or 'beware Satan.'", "reasons": "Abu Muslim connects to the preceding warning against Satan; Abu Hayyan and Samīn give an omitted 'turn' or 'approach' command. Alusi lists this proposal too."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q05", "question": "What does 'establish your faces' direct worshippers to do?", "turns_on": "The force of 'face' and 'mosque': bodily qibla, wholehearted orientation, the mosque reached, congregation, universal prayer place, Meccan sanctuary, or inward station. Razi and Tabatabai give explicit textual and historical objections.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q05/p1", "position": "Face the Kaaba or divinely prescribed qibla in prayer wherever prayer occurs.", "reasons": "Mujahid explicitly includes church and other places. Muqatil includes mosque, church and synagogue; Ibn Atiyya calls qibla adherence required. Tabarsi's Jubbai glosses the prescribed direction and prayer times; Alusi says many call it obligatory. Razi prefers this because sincerity is expressed separately and rejects the duplicate sincerity reading. Tabatabai calls qibla reports an application and links 2:144; he rejects making it the primary Meccan sense because the Kaaba became qibla in Medina, though allows this verse's general command later specified. Study Quran cites 2:144 and 2:150."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p2", "position": "Turn wholly and uprightly toward God in worship, intention, and prayer, without other objects of devotion.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi treats 'face' as aim rather than organ; Baydawi, Nasafi, Zamakhshari, Alusi and Tabatabai stress undivided attention. Ibn Ashur compares facing an important sight without looking aside and explains 'establish' as firm action (2:3, 30:30); worship is reverent (hadith forbidding spitting before oneself). Abu al-Aliya combines exclusive devotion with facing the Sacred House. Ibn Kathir adds following messengers' law and freedom from shirk as the two conditions of acceptance. Elmalili calls for uniform communal orientation. Study Quran gives parallels at 2:112, 3:20, 6:79, 10:105, 30:30, 30:43 and 31:22. Tabatabai prefers wholehearted ritual orientation, but calls a mere sincerity gloss incomplete since the next clause repeats it."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p3", "position": "Pray at the mosque where the time of praye

Tabatabai objects that multiple Muslim mosques do not fit the Meccan setting."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p4", "position": "Attend a mosque for every prayer and pray with the congregation.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Tabarsi say most regard congregation as recommended, a minority obligatory; Alusi repeats the split. Biqai extends orientation to every suitable place, time and circumstance."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p6", "position": "The command first addresses exclusive worship at pilgrimage sanctuaries, rejecting idols and naked ritual.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the Meccan audience then had pilgrimage sanctuaries rather than later mosques; Hubal was on the Kaaba, Isaf and Naila at Safa and Marwa, and Manat at al-Mushallal. Believers are to continue observing the command."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p7", "position": "An inward discipline of uprightness at each spiritual station of prostration.", "reasons": "Junayd calls for guarding the secret, raising aspiration and contentment in God. Qashani restrains excess, deficiency and spiritual fluctuation; his four stations are obedience, annihilation in actions, annihilation in attributes and annihilation in essence, each with conditions and dangers."}, {"id": "7:29/q05/p8", "position": "A report takes the established faces to be the Imams, which Tabatabai understands as congregational prayer leaders.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq supplies the report; Tabatabai notes another possible sense follows."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q06", "question": "What can 'face' and 'at every mosque' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether masjid functions as a place noun, time noun, or metonym for prayer or worship; whether wajh is bodily direction or whole-person attention.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q06/p1", "position": "Face can mean one's aim, attention, or whole being, beyond the physical organ.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explains al-Rabi's aim rather than organ; Asad cites 3:20, and Ibn Ashur pictures full attention to an important sight."}, {"id": "7:29/q06/p2", "position": "Masjid denotes a place of prostration or a mosque, including any designated place of worship.", "reasons": "Farra and Tabarsi take the place; Ibn Ashur distinguishes general places set aside for worship from the later specific bounded Islamic prayer building, citing 5:2. Samīn notes the irregular kasra pattern where fatḥa is expected, with many analogues. Alusi says ʿinda can mean 'in' and sajda names prayer by a part."}, {"id": "7:29/q06/p3", "position": "Masjid denotes the time of prostration or prayer, each prayer occasion.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi's Abu Ishaq say each prayer time; Razi prefers the time-based sense over the place-based one; Jubbai, Zamakhshari, Samīn, Alusi, Elmalili and Bursawi allow it. Sujud may name the whole prayer, a part for the whole."}, {"id": "7:29/q06/p4", "position": "Here masjid can extend to every act of worship, not merely a time or place.", "reasons": "Asad compares 7:31; Qashani makes stations of prostration inward stages."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q07", "question": "What occasion or practical ruling is associated with praying at each mosque?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording imposes attendance or direction, and whether congregational prayer is recommended or obligatory.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q07/p1", "position": "People once refused other mosques in favor of their own; the verse tells them to pray where the time finds them.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports the occasion as preference for their own mosque and qibla. Farra, Dahhak, Ibn Qutayba and others urge the available mosque. Razi denies that the verse actually prohibits moving between mosques; Tabatabai says this presupposes multiple Muslim mosques absent in Mecca."}, {"id": "7:29/q07/p2", "position": "Congregational mosque prayer is recommended according to most, obligatory according to a minority.", "reasons": "Mawrdi, Tabarsi and Alusi give this split. Haddadi argues obligation with an exemption for those with an excuse who hear the call. Bursawi says mosque congregation better displays Islam's symbols for obligatory prayer and tarawih; home congregation is better than praying alone at home. The nearby mosque can be preferred when its imam is learned."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q08", "question": "What does 'call upon Him' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether duʿa names worship or formal prayer broadly, literal petition, or confession of oneness.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q08/p1", "position": "Worship God, including ritual prayer and remembrance.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursawi, Ibn Ashur and others give worship. Razi prefers prayer because salat literally means supplication and its noblest acts are petition and remembrance; Bursawi says a particular act names the broader worship, whose gateway is humble need. Ibn Ashur cites 7:194, and Alusi says worship includes prayer."}, {"id": "7:29/q08/p2", "position": "Supplicate God, asking Him alone after purifying one's religion.", "reasons": "Mawrdi, Ibn Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi report petition; Tabarsi holds humble petition after sincere religion; Study Quran says petitions commonly concern spiritual and material needs and Abu Hayyan adds exclusive devotion as a condition of response."}, {"id": "7:29/q08/p3", "position": "Say the testimony of God's oneness and invoke no other deity.", "reasons": "Muqatil joins prayer and monotheism; Wahidi and Qurtubi take it as affirmation without partners. Abu Hayyan lists the shahada as a possible meaning."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q09", "question": "What is meant by sincerity in religion to Him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q09/p1", "position": "Devote worship and obedience purely to God, without idols, partners, hypocrisy, or ostentation.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Baghawi gloss din as obedience/worship; Baydawi, Bursawi and Ibn Ashur stress obedience because all return to God. Tabarsi derives ikhlas from removing admixture; Ibn Ashur calls din obedience and explains the divine name al-Dayyan. Razi says sincerity covers both preceding commands because din embraces every devotion, comparing 98:5; Ibn Ashur likewise uses 98:5 to eliminate association. Nasafi says act seeking God's face; Qashani's first station avoids hypocrisy and his later stations see obedience as from and through God. Study Quran cites recurring formula at 10:22, 29:65, 31:32, 39:2, 39:11, 39:14, 40:14, 40:65, 73:8. Islahi says worship and obedience belong to God alone (72:18)."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q10", "question": "How is 'sincere to Him in religion' construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q10/p1", "position": "Mukhlisin is a circumstantial accusative modifying the callers, and al-din is its object.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Samīn give the construction; Samīn allows lahu either to attach to mukhlisin or modify al-din circumstantially. Ibn Ashur links the circumstantial phrase to the pronoun in 'call/worship Him.'"}]}
{"id": "7:29/q11", "question": "What inward states make invocation sincere?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q11/p1", "position": "Conceal self-regard and ostentation, watch God continuously, and let all dealings be with Him alone.", "reasons": "Tustari advises private examination because only the sincere recognize showing off; outward conduct follows the Prophet, otherwise it is astray. {"id": "7:29/q12", "question": "What do 'began' and 'return' mean as words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q12/p1", "position": "To begin is to originate or perform first; to return is to perform again or restore.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi distinguish first and second performance, with Jishumi calling God initiator/restorer and qualifying what can be restored. Abu Hayyan glosses badaʾa as originate/invent; Samīn says triliteral badaʾa and quadriliteral abdaʾa both occur (29:19–20), and with baʾ it can mean place first; Raghib records a rare abdaʾtu form, while abdaʾtu min ard means start departing. Samīn records badʾ as a chief counted first, with two anonymous poetic examples, one leader after his people died and one master not previously made master. Burhan says the triliteral is more eloquent but the paired quadriliteral yubdiʾ/yuʿid creates correspondence; beginning then return follows temporal order among Quranic pairs."}]}

{"id": "7:29/q14", "question": "In what sense will people return as God began them?", "turns_on": "The compared feature of beginning and return: renewed life, primordial division and decree, state at death, earthly origin, lack of possessions, original fitra, or inward annihilation. A wisdom report in Durr counsels against boasting and arrogance because God lowers the arrogant and raises the oppressed."}, {"id": "7:29/q14/p5", "position": "People return possessing nothing, barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised as when born.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports an Ibn Abbas tradition adding Abraham is first clothed (21:104); Ibn Kathir says the Prophetic report is in both Sahihs, also al-Bukhari via Thawri. This can be understood with the two destiny groups but emphasizes knowledge/writing as the return's object."}, {"id": "7:29/q14/p8", "position": "The beginning is hidden manifestation by God; the return is annihilation in Him so He alone appears.", "reasons": "Qashani gives this inward account, continuous with his stations of annihilation in actions, attributes and essence."}, {"id": "7:29/q14/p9", "position": "A report says the verse's promised return will occur at the end of this community.", "reasons": "Durr transmits Muqatil ibn Wahb's statement without further explanation."}, {"id": "7:29/q14/p10", "position": "A report describes some sinners transformed in this world, then raised human before entering Hell.", "reasons": "Durr attributes this to the Prophet via a citation of al-Bukhari's al-Duʿafaʾ; the sin is private contempt of God."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q15", "question": "Does the two-group return entail fixed and inescapable fate?", "turns_on": "Whether prior division or material endowment is a complete cause of an individual's end, or a general decree realized through voluntary response.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q15/p1", "position": "The original decree determines the final happy or wretched group, even when intermediate deeds look opposite.", "reasons": "Quraẓī uses Iblis and the sorcerers; Sulami's Husayn says the decree about deeds does not change. Ibn Atiyya invokes unchanging divine decrees. Alusi transmits a Tirmidhi report from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs: two registers for Paradise and Hell are shown; companions are told to strive because final deeds decide the outcome. Qushayri describes matched original disposition, state and end."}, {"id": "7:29/q15/p2", "position": "The original two-group decree is general and conditional; persons reach outcomes through chosen allegiance and deeds.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reads 15:42, 22:4, 38:84 and 20:123–124: Satan leads those who follow him, not an independently forced class. Ibn Kathir says original fitra is common while belief and disbelief arise later (30:30, 64:2, 87:3, 20:50)."}, {"id": "7:29/q15/p3", "position": "Initial material constitution predisposes human traits but does not completely cause belief or fate.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reports Sajjad's high clay for Shia, Sijjin for enemies and lower clay for their allies; Sadiq's mixed Paradise/Fire clay explains good non-Shia and bad Shia; Ali's varied earth yields righteous and wicked descendants. {"id": "7:29/q17", "question": "What does the adjacent division into two parties explain about this return?", "turns_on": "Whether 7:30 supplies the comparison's very point of likeness or functions chiefly as the moral consequence of the commands.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q17/p1", "position": "The next verse specifies return in two parties, guided and astray, reflecting humanity's first division.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Durr, Biqai and Tabatabai connect 7:30 to the phrase; Ubayy's reading explicitly inserts the two parties. {"id": "7:29/q18", "question": "How are the two parties and 'error became due' expressed in the adjoining wording?", "turns_on": "The syntactic role of the two-party phrases and whether masculine agreement is grammatical license or a semantic signal of punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q18/p1", "position": "The two party phrases can be accusative objects or circumstantial expressions qualifying the return.", "reasons": "Majaz says both fariqan forms are accusative under the verb, the second coordinated by proximity without sharing sense, citing 76:31. {"id": "7:29/q19", "question": "What do the cited readings contribute to this passage?", "turns_on": "Whether a cited form is an attested reading that can clarify the two groups or a later unsupported reconstruction.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q19/p1", "position": "Ubayy's wording explicitly reads the return as two groups, one guided and one astray.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan cite it in support of the two-group interpretation; Abu Hayyan says the second group is circumstantial."}, {"id": "7:29/q19/p2", "position": "A reading is not anomalous merely because it lies outside the Seven or famous manuals; invented Hamza stop forms are invalid.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari rejects calling everything outside the Seven, Shatibiyya or Taysir anomalous, and rejects later commentators' supposed rasm-based Hamza-stop yāʾ, wāw, alif substitutions and deletions. {"id": "7:29/q20", "question": "What other language or comparisons are adduced near this verse?", "turns_on": "The cited material ranges from comparison theory and grammatical shifts to lexical notes on neighboring text.", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q20/p1", "position": "The comparison particle can express an intellectual likeness rather than bodily or sensory resemblance.", "reasons": "Jurjani's Prophetic 'green growth on dung' compares attractive beauty from bad upbringing with outwardly appealing growth rooted in corruption, not plant color, taste, smell or form. Honey's sweetness and bitterness analogize joy at agreement and distress at opposition. Calling a man 'sun' transfers eminence, rank, honor and fame; 'stars of guidance' likens Companions' teaching and example to celestial navigation. These are general analogies adduced in discussion of comparison."}, {"id": "7:29/q20/p2", "position": "The verse illustrates a shift from past statement to imperative.", "reasons": "Burhan pairs 'my Lord commanded justice' with 'establish your faces' and cites a command after the permissibility of cattle as another example."}, {"id": "7:29/q20/p3", "position": "Other nearby lexical examples explain high crests, the older form of 'six,' and an exhortation verb.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites poetry for aʿraf as a high place, mountain crest and upright lances, and notes horse and rooster crests; explains six from sidsa by consonant change and assimilation, preserved in its diminutive; and reports Layth's 'exhorting' as hastening someone, whose agent is eager or urged. These notes concern adjacent vocabulary rather than 7:29's words."}]}
{"id": "7:29/q21", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding passage as a whole?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:29/q21/p1", "position": "It replaces a false divine command with true religion: justice, upright worship, exclusive devotion, and accountable return.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says 7:28's denial is followed by an emphatic repeated 'say' and foundations of true religion; Biqai, Razi, Elmalili and Kuranyolu describe the sequence. Ibn Ashur says the initially addressed polytheists must abandon invented rites and believers maintain the command. Islahi's broader sura reading addresses Adam's children to remind Quraysh and Arabs that Satan is humanity's enduring enemy and following him befriends their father's foe."}]}

{"id": "7:91/q03", "question": "What happened when the punishment struck?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on the order and agents of destruction: fire, cry, earthquake, lightning, withheld wind, or a falling mountain.", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q03/p1", "position": "Heat drove them beneath a cooling cloud, which burned them as the earth shook.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and others describe unbearable heat, useless shelter or caves, a cool or fragrant cloud, then fire and earthquake, leaving ash or fried-locust-like bodies. {"id": "7:91/q04", "question": "How do the quake, cry, and Day of the Canopy accounts relate?", "turns_on": "Whether the Qur'anic descriptions are concurrent elements or causes of one disaster, or belong to distinct communities; al-Ālūsī tests the latter against 11:94.", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q04/p1", "position": "The punishments happened together to the same people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr links Hūd's blast (11:94), the mockery of Shuʿayb's prayer (11:87), their demand for a falling piece of heaven (26:187), and the day of shade (26:189). Iṣlāḥī says Hūd 11:94 supplies a shout and thunder, while 26:189 describes a canopy looking from afar like a column or mountain of dust or smoke; he treats the ḥāṣib as combining rajfah, ṣayḥah and ẓullah. Study Quran's report combines fire, cry, and quake."}, {"id": "7:91/q04/p2", "position": "The cry preceded the quake, so the two descriptions name stages or causes of one event.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī cites al-Ḥijr 15:73 as calling it a cry and suggests onset; Bursawī cites Hūd's cry and calls it near versus remote cause. Al-Biqāʿī allows the quake to result from the cry, or the reverse."}, {"id": "7:91/q04/p3", "position": "The quake was an earthquake, and the cry was the thunderbolt accompanying lightning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr argues from Hūd 11:94 that the sound was a splitting burst from one thing launched against another, rather than the impact of an earthquake; he prefers simultaneous earthquake and lightning, consistent with erased traces."}, {"id": "7:91/q04/p4", "position": "Different groups of Shuʿayb's people suffered the earthquake and the canopy.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah offers separate groups as an alternative to simultaneous events; al-Ṭabrisī reports a two-peoples version, one destroyed by quake and one by canopy; Abū Ḥayyān transmits Ibn ʿAṭiyyah."}, {"id": "7:91/q04/p5", "position": "The accounts give distinct punishments to Midian and the people of the Thicket.", "reasons": "Qatāda assigns the cry of Gabriel to Midian and the canopy to the Thicket, as do ʿIkrima and al-Suddī, who say Shuʿayb was sent twice. {"id": "7:91/q05", "question": "Were Midian and the people of al-Aykah one people or two?", "turns_on": "Whether Shuʿayb's mission addressed one community or two, and whether a single people could receive both the cry and the quake.", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q05/p1", "position": "Two peoples received Shuʿayb, with different modes of destruction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports this possibility; Qatāda says the Thicket had the shade and Midian Gabriel's shout. ʿIkrima and al-Suddī say Shuʿayb was sent twice. {"id": "7:91/q06", "question": "What does aṣbaḥū indicate here?", "turns_on": "Whether aṣbaḥa marks actual morning or simply entry into a state.", "positions": [{"id": "7:91/q06/p1", "position": "Morning came upon them in this state.", "reasons": "Jishumī says aṣbaḥa means to enter morning as amsā means to enter evening; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows that morning came upon them and points to the parallel account in 7:78."}, {"id": "7:91/q06/p2", "position": "They became so, without necessarily specifying morning.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this as the other sense and refers to his earlier explanation at Ṣāliḥ's parallel in 7:78."}]}
